title: Terroir Deep Dive
description: A rigorous scientific exploration of Burgundy's terroir — from Jurassic limestone geology and soil chemistry to microclimate analysis and how all these forces manifest in the glass.
lessons.0.title: The Science of Terroir
lessons.0.slides.0.title: The Science of Terroir
lessons.0.slides.0.subtitle: 20 minutes
lessons.0.slides.0.description: Move beyond the romantic notion of terroir to understand the precise scientific mechanisms — soil, geology, climate and biology — that make each Burgundy parcel unique.
lessons.0.slides.1.title: Defining Terroir Scientifically
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Terroir is not magic — it is a measurable interaction of physical, chemical and biological factors that influence grape physiology and ultimately wine character. Modern soil science, climatology and plant biology have begun to explain what centuries of vineyard observation recorded empirically.
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Geology: parent rock type, age and fracture patterns determine mineral availability and drainage architecture
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Soil: texture, depth, organic matter, pH and cation exchange capacity shape root development and nutrient uptake
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Microclimate: slope, aspect, elevation and surrounding vegetation modify temperature, humidity and frost risk
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Biology: soil microbial communities (bacteria, mycorrhizal fungi) mediate nutrient cycling and stress responses
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.4: Human factor: planting density, pruning systems and the accumulated knowledge of generations of vignerons
lessons.0.slides.2.title: 🔬 Soil Chemistry Basics
lessons.0.slides.2.content: Understanding soil chemistry is essential for interpreting why adjacent parcels produce wines of markedly different character — even when farmed and vinified identically.
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.0: pH: Burgundy soils typically range 7.0–8.0 (slightly alkaline); alkalinity from limestone affects iron availability and vine stress
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC): measures the soil's ability to retain calcium, magnesium, potassium and micronutrients; higher CEC = more nutrient buffer
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Active limestone (calcaire actif): the proportion of calcium carbonate in reactive form; high active limestone can cause iron chlorosis in susceptible rootstocks
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Organic matter: contributes to water retention, microbial activity and slow-release nitrogen — critical in shallow soils
lessons.0.slides.3.title: 🌿 Microbial Life and Terroir Expression
lessons.0.slides.3.content: The rhizosphere — the zone of soil immediately surrounding vine roots — is home to a complex ecosystem of microorganisms that profoundly influence vine health and terroir transmission.
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Mycorrhizal fungi: form symbiotic networks with vine roots, extending their effective reach up to 100× and facilitating mineral uptake
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Bacteria: nitrogen-fixing bacteria improve available nitrogen; others produce growth hormones or suppress pathogens
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Soil microbiome and wine microbiology: some researchers propose that indigenous yeast populations in the cellar reflect the vineyard's microbial signature
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Biodynamic and organic farming enhance microbial diversity; conventional tillage and herbicide use reduce it
lessons.0.slides.4.title: 💡 Key Takeaways
lessons.0.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 Terroir is a measurable scientific interaction — not mysticism
lessons.0.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 Soil pH, CEC and active limestone content are the primary chemical drivers of parcel differentiation
lessons.0.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 Mycorrhizal networks and soil microbial communities mediate mineral uptake and may link vineyard to cellar
lessons.0.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 Biodynamic farming measurably increases soil biological diversity
lessons.0.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.question: What is 'cation exchange capacity' (CEC) in a vineyard context?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.0: A. A measure of how much sun a slope receives per day
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.1: B. The soil's ability to retain and supply positively charged nutrient ions to vine roots
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.2: C. The number of mycorrhizal fungi per cubic metre of soil
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.3: D. A French legal classification for Grand Cru soils
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: CEC (Cation Exchange Capacity) measures how well a soil can hold positively charged ions — calcium, magnesium, potassium, ammonium — that vines need. High CEC soils act as nutrient buffers, releasing ions gradually rather than losing them in rainfall. Clay-rich soils have high CEC; sandy soils have low CEC. In Burgundy, the balance of clay and limestone in different parcels is a key reason adjacent plots produce different wines.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.question: What role do mycorrhizal fungi play in terroir expression?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.options.0: A. They ferment grape juice in the cellar
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.options.1: B. They form networks with vine roots that extend mineral uptake reach and may transmit the vineyard's mineral signature to the grape
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.options.2: C. They suppress all other soil organisms
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.options.3: D. They are irrelevant to vine growth and terroir
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: Mycorrhizal fungi form symbiotic relationships with plant roots, vastly extending their effective surface area for water and mineral absorption. In a healthy organic or biodynamic vineyard, these networks can extend the vine's reach up to 100 times beyond the root itself. There is growing scientific evidence that the mineral signature of a soil — mediated through these networks — influences the mineral flavour character perceived in wine. Herbicide use (glyphosate in particular) is known to disrupt mycorrhizal networks.
lessons.1.title: Burgundy's Geological Foundation
lessons.1.slides.0.title: Burgundy's Geological Foundation
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: 18 minutes
lessons.1.slides.0.description: The Côte d'Or sits on a complex Jurassic geological patchwork — understanding the formation and age of each stratum is the key to understanding why individual parcels taste different.
lessons.1.slides.1.title: Jurassic Rock: The Foundation
lessons.1.slides.1.content: Burgundy's Côte d'Or sits on rocks laid down during the Jurassic period (200–145 million years ago), when the region was a warm shallow sea. The alternating layers of limestone and marl are the geological engine behind the region's extraordinary terroir diversity.
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Jurassic origin: most Côte d'Or bedrock dates to Middle and Late Jurassic (Bajocian to Tithonian stages)
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Limestone (calcaire): hard, free-draining, high in calcium carbonate; dominates upper and mid-slopes
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Marl (marne): limestone + clay mix; softer, water-retentive, nutrient-rich; tends toward lower slopes and valley floors
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Fault system: the Saône graben — a rift valley — lifted and exposed different rock strata on the escarpment, creating the variety of soil types we see today
lessons.1.slides.2.title: 🏔️ Key Geological Stages
lessons.1.slides.2.content: Different stages of the Jurassic period produced different rock types, and the exposed strata shift as you move along the Côte d'Or. This is why Gevrey, Chambolle and Vosne differ despite being only kilometres apart.
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Bajocian (174–168 Ma): compact oolitic limestone — creates well-drained soils with good structure; common in Gevrey-Chambertin mid-slopes
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Bathonian (168–166 Ma): alternating limestone and marl — the classic 'Burgundy' combination; dominates many Premiers and Grands Crus
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Callovian / Oxfordian (166–157 Ma): richer in clay and marl; tends to give wines with more body and structure
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Kimmeridgian (157–152 Ma): the key stage for Chablis (see Module 4); compact limestone rich in tiny fossilised oysters
lessons.1.slides.3.title: 🗺️ The Côte d'Or Fault Scarp
lessons.1.slides.3.content: The topography of the Côte d'Or — the westward-facing escarpment overlooking the Saône plain — is the direct result of tectonic faulting that began 30 million years ago and tilted Jurassic rock to the surface.
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.0: The Saône graben: a geological rift valley that dropped the land to the east, leaving the Côte d'Or as a raised escarpment
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Slope = drainage: the inclined strata allow rainwater to drain downhill, preventing waterlogging at mid-slopes (where Grands Crus tend to sit)
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Erosion and colluvium: over millennia, rock has broken down and washed downhill, creating a surface mantle of mixed soils over the parent bedrock
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.3: East-southeast aspect: the fault scarp orientation maximises afternoon sun exposure while the Morvan hills to the west provide shelter from rain-bearing westerly winds
lessons.1.slides.4.title: 💡 Key Takeaways
lessons.1.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 The Côte d'Or's soils are Jurassic in origin — 150–170 million years old
lessons.1.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 Limestone dominates upper slopes (drainage, minerality); marl dominates lower slopes (body, richness)
lessons.1.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 The fault scarp creates the slope, aspect and drainage conditions that define Grand Cru quality zones
lessons.1.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 Different Jurassic stages (Bajocian, Bathonian, Callovian) explain why adjacent villages taste so different
lessons.1.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.question: What geological event created the topography of the Côte d'Or escarpment?
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.options.0: A. A volcanic eruption that deposited basalt over Jurassic limestone
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.options.1: B. Glacial activity during the last Ice Age that carved the valley
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.options.2: C. Tectonic faulting (the Saône graben) that dropped land to the east, exposing Jurassic strata on a sloping escarpment
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.options.3: D. Fluvial erosion by the Saône river over millions of years
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: The Côte d'Or's characteristic escarpment — a raised, south-east facing slope — was created by tectonic faulting approximately 30 million years ago. The Saône graben (a rift valley) subsided to the east, leaving Jurassic limestone strata tilted and exposed to form the slope. This fault structure is the origin of the ideal drainage and sun exposure that define Grand Cru terroir — the best parcels occupy the mid-slope where drainage is optimal and sun exposure is maximised.
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.question: Why do Grand Cru vineyards typically sit on mid-slopes rather than at the top or bottom of the Côte d'Or?
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.options.0: A. Medieval monks chose the most accessible terrain
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.options.1: B. Mid-slopes offer optimal drainage (avoiding waterlogging), ideal sun exposure and the best limestone-to-clay soil ratio
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.options.2: C. Lower slopes have deeper soils that produce more concentrated wines
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.options.3: D. AOC law requires Grands Crus to be planted at specific altitudes
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: The mid-slope position on the Côte d'Or combines several advantages: excellent drainage (excess water runs downhill rather than pooling), maximum sun exposure (the Côte faces east/south-east), thin soils over limestone bedrock (which stress the vine and concentrate flavour), and protection from frost (cold air drains to the valley floor). Flat valley bottoms have heavy clay soils and frost risk; hilltops have too-thin soils, wind exposure and insufficient heat accumulation. The mid-slope 'sweet spot' is where Burgundy's Grands Crus are concentrated.
lessons.2.title: Microclimate and Topography
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Microclimate and Topography
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: 15 minutes
lessons.2.slides.0.description: How slope angle, aspect, elevation and surrounding vegetation create micro-environments that differ significantly from general weather station data — and why this matters for Grand Cru quality.
lessons.2.slides.1.title: What is Microclimate?
lessons.2.slides.1.content: Microclimate refers to the local atmospheric conditions of a specific small area — often differing substantially from regional averages. In Burgundy, adjacent vineyards 100 metres apart can have measurably different temperature regimes, humidity levels and frost risk profiles.
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Temperature: south-east aspect absorbs morning sun early; slopes retain heat longer than flat land
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Frost: cold air is denser than warm air and drains to valley floors — mid-slope Grand Cru sites are often 2–3°C warmer on cold nights than the village below
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Humidity: forests and hedgerows above vineyards can trap moisture; good air circulation reduces disease pressure
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Wind: the Morvan hills provide a natural windbreak from Atlantic rain-bearing westerlies, creating a rain shadow over the Côte d'Or
lessons.2.slides.2.title: ⛰️ Slope Angle and Aspect
lessons.2.slides.2.content: In Burgundy, even small differences in slope and aspect have been shown to produce significantly different ripening profiles. This partly explains why a Grand Cru can neighbour a Village-level parcel yet produce dramatically superior wine.
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Optimal angle: 10–15° slope maximises sun incidence on the Côte d'Or's east-facing escarpment
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Steeper slopes: better drainage, less soil depth, more stress on vines — often associated with greater minerality and structure
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Flatter sections within Grand Cru boundaries: often demoted within producer blends because ripening is less consistent
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Clos de Vougeot example: 51 hectares from near-flat valley floor to well-drained mid-slope — wines from different parts of the parcel taste markedly different
lessons.2.slides.3.title: 🌡️ Heat Accumulation and Growing Degree Days
lessons.2.slides.3.content: Growing Degree Days (GDD) measure accumulated heat above 10°C during the growing season — a key tool for comparing vintages and understanding site differences.
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.0: GDD formula: sum of daily (max temp + min temp)/2 − 10°C for each day above 10°C base
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Burgundy averages ~1,200–1,400 GDD — at the lower end of successful wine production, explaining vintage sensitivity
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Climate change impact: Burgundy's GDD has increased by ~150–200 GDD over the past 30 years, shifting the vintage calendar forward by ~2 weeks
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Site differences: a south-facing mid-slope may accumulate 5–10% more GDD than a flat parcel 200m away
lessons.2.slides.4.title: 💡 Key Takeaways
lessons.2.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 Microclimate creates measurable differences between adjacent parcels — frost risk, temperature, humidity
lessons.2.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 Mid-slope sites drain cold air downhill — a critical frost-protection mechanism for Grands Crus
lessons.2.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 Growing Degree Days quantify heat accumulation — Burgundy sits at the marginal threshold of ~1,200–1,400 GDD
lessons.2.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 Climate change has added ~150–200 GDD over 30 years, fundamentally shifting vintage dynamics
lessons.2.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.question: Why do mid-slope Grand Cru sites have lower frost risk than the village floor below?
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.options.0: A. They receive more direct sunlight which keeps soil temperatures higher
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.options.1: B. Cold air, being denser, drains downhill to the valley floor — mid-slope sites sit above the coldest frost pocket
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.options.2: C. AOC regulations require frost protection systems in all Grand Cru vineyards
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.options.3: D. Stone walls surrounding Grands Crus retain heat and prevent frost
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: Cold air is denser than warm air and, on still, clear nights (the most dangerous frost conditions), flows downhill like water and collects in hollows and valley floors. Mid-slope positions — characteristic of Burgundy's Grands Crus — sit above the coldest frost drainage zones. This is why, on nights of spring frost (April–May is most critical in Burgundy), a mid-slope parcel may be 2–4°C warmer than the flat land below. This is one of the key physical reasons why the Grands Crus occupy their specific topographic positions.
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.question: Burgundy averages approximately how many Growing Degree Days (GDD) per season?
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: Burgundy accumulates approximately 1,200–1,400 GDD per season, placing it at the lower end of the temperature threshold for reliable grape ripening (generally considered ~1,100 GDD minimum). This 'marginal' heat accumulation is precisely why Burgundy is so vintage-sensitive — a warmer summer shifts GDD to 1,500–1,600 (producing richer, more opulent wines like 2015), while a cool summer near 1,100 GDD creates lean, acidic wines or crop failures. Climate change has increased average GDD by ~150–200 over 30 years, fundamentally altering Burgundy's vintage character.
lessons.3.title: Reading Terroir in the Glass
lessons.3.slides.0.title: Reading Terroir in the Glass
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: 15 minutes
lessons.3.slides.0.description: How the geological, chemical and climatic forces studied in this module manifest as flavour, texture and structure in wine — and how to identify terroir signatures in professional tasting.
lessons.3.slides.1.title: From Soil to Glass: The Transmission Pathway
lessons.3.slides.1.content: The connection between soil minerals and wine flavour is one of the most debated topics in oenology. While no mineral ion survives fermentation unchanged, the indirect effects of soil chemistry on vine physiology and stress response are well documented.
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Vine stress: shallow limestone soils force deep root development; moderate water stress concentrates flavour and aroma compounds
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Mineral uptake: potassium levels in soils influence wine pH and acid perception; calcium availability affects tartrate stability
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Aroma chemistry: volatile thiols, terpenes and lactones that contribute 'mineral' flavours may reflect vine metabolism responses to soil conditions
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.3: The 'rocky-wet-stone' aroma: often associated with Chablis Grands Crus and Puligny-Montrachet — likely reflects a combination of reductive winemaking and specific volatile compound profiles
lessons.3.slides.2.title: 🍷 Terroir Signatures by Region
lessons.3.slides.2.content: Experienced tasters identify characteristic terroir signatures for specific communes and Grands Crus. While subjective, these are grounded in measurable soil and climatic differences.
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Gevrey-Chambertin: power, iron, dark fruit, spice — deeper clay-limestone soils, relatively fertile, produces structured red wines
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Chambolle-Musigny: perfume, delicacy, rose petal, pure red fruit — lighter, limestone-dominant soils, less clay
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Vosne-Romanée: silky texture, violet, spice, 'perfect balance' — complex soil mix of limestone, gravel and clay at DRC sites
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Puligny-Montrachet: citrus pith, flint, white flowers, tension — thin soils over limestone, cool aspect
lessons.3.slides.3.title: 🏅 Clos de Vougeot: Terroir Within a Grand Cru
lessons.3.slides.3.content: The 51-hectare Clos de Vougeot is divided among 80+ producers. Tasting across different producers' wines reveals the dramatic influence of parcel position within a single Grand Cru.
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Upper slope (near Musigny): thin limestone soils, excellent drainage — produces elegant, perfumed, long-lived wines; prized parcels
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Middle slope: balanced limestone-clay; considered the 'typical' expression of Clos de Vougeot — rich, structured
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Lower slope (near RN74 road): heavy clay soils, poor drainage, flat terrain — often produces coarser, earthier wine; lower prices
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Many top producers declassify lower-slope fruit to Premier Cru level voluntarily — the most rigorous interpretation of Grand Cru quality
lessons.3.slides.4.title: 💡 Key Takeaways
lessons.3.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 No mineral ion survives fermentation — terroir expresses itself through vine physiology and stress response
lessons.3.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 Each major commune has a recognisable flavour signature grounded in measurable soil differences
lessons.3.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 Clos de Vougeot demonstrates that even within a Grand Cru, parcel position creates dramatic quality variation
lessons.3.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 The best producers voluntarily declassify lower-quality parcels — the ultimate expression of terroir respect
lessons.3.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.0.question: Why does Chambolle-Musigny typically produce more delicate, perfumed Pinot Noir than the more powerful wines of Gevrey-Chambertin?
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.0.options.0: A. Chambolle uses different clonal selections
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.0.options.1: B. Chambolle's soils are lighter, with more limestone and less clay than Gevrey's deeper, more clay-rich soils
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.0.options.2: C. Gevrey producers deliberately make bigger wines through longer maceration
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.0.options.3: D. Chambolle receives less sunlight due to its northerly position
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: The soil difference is the primary explanation. Chambolle-Musigny sits on predominantly limestone soils with relatively little clay, producing thin, well-drained soils. This creates vine stress that produces wines with delicate, ethereal textures and pronounced floral aromatics. Gevrey-Chambertin has deeper soils with a higher clay content, particularly in its famous plots near the village. This deeper, richer soil profile produces wines with more body, darker fruit, firmer tannin and a characteristic iron-like mineral quality — the archetypal 'powerful' Gevrey style.
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.question: Producers who voluntarily declassify lower-slope Clos de Vougeot fruit to Premier Cru level are demonstrating which principle?
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.options.0: A. Legal compliance with INAO regulations
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.options.1: B. A commitment to Grand Cru quality standards above legal entitlement — using only the best parcels for the top label
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.options.2: C. Maximising profit by selling Premier Cru at higher prices
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.options.3: D. Following the Burgundy appellation's mandatory declassification rules
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: Producers like Méo-Camuzet, Leroy and Mugnier who own parcels in the lower Clos de Vougeot (near the N74 road) often chose to blend this fruit into their Bourgogne or Vosne-Romanée rather than labelling it as Grand Cru. There is no legal requirement to do so — they are entitled to use the Grand Cru appellation on all fruit from the Clos. This voluntary declassification is considered the highest expression of terroir integrity: Grand Cru quality is earned, not merely inherited from map coordinates.
lessons.3.slides.6.title: Module Summary
lessons.3.slides.6.content: Burgundy's terroir is not a vague poetic concept — it is a precise intersection of Jurassic geology, soil chemistry, topographic microclimate and biological activity. Understanding these mechanisms allows the student to move from 'this wine tastes different' to 'this wine expresses specific forces operating on this exact piece of ground for 150 million years'. That is the foundation of expert Burgundy appreciation.
